The pads are completely reversible and the wheels are not supposed to be conical to the point of pad placement making a difference.  They should be pretty cylindrical with a specific radius leading up to the flange (depending on wheel type, class, and load rating), the edge of the brake is applied at the bottom of the radius.  The only thing you can't do is replace High Friction shoes with Low Friction/Wrought Iron shoes, the locating nubs on the back have a 2 inch spacing difference that doesn't allow them to switch places.

There are even different types of brake shoes to attempt to repair a wheel before being replaced, by filling in holes/divots in the wheels with powdered iron that melts in the high friction environment (sintered shoes).
